title: Topological Sort and Cycle Detection
excerpt: Given a pile of tasks with dependencies, find an order that respects all of them. The algorithm is what you would do by hand, and it detects the impossible cases for free.
seoTitle: Topological Sort: Kahn's Algorithm and Cycle Detection
seoDescription: Topological sorting derived: why a cycle makes ordering impossible, how in-degree counting gives Kahn's algorithm, a full trace, the DFS finish-time alternative, and why the output is rarely unique.

content.text: Topological sorting is a linear ordering of vertices for Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs), such that for every directed edge from vertex u to vertex v, u appears before v in the ordering.
Suppose the graph has a cycle: A before B, B before C, C before A. No ordering is possible because all nodes must come before each other.

On the other hand, every graph with no cycles (a DAG) always has a topological ordering. This is because a DAG has at least one node with an in-degree of zero. From this, we can "peel" nodes off layer by layer without violating any dependency rules.

To start, we can push all the nodes with in-degree 0 to the stack, and remove it from the DAG. Once remove these nodes from the DAG, the nodes it used to point to are now of in-degree 0, and they too can be pushed to the stack, and removed from the graph. Continue doing this until no nodes remain, and the stack now contains a valid topological ordering.

This is Kahn's algorithm—not only can it create topological orderings—it can also detect cycles. If the algorithm finishes with a stack that has fewer nodes than the graph contains, no nodes left contain an in-degree of zero, therefore there must be a cycle. An implementation of Kahn's algorithm is found in the sections below.

body.text: The other way to do it

content.text: If you need to do a depth-first search anyway, you can also use it to create a topological sorting.
Run a DFS on every node in the DAG. When a node
finishes
, meaning you have fully explored everything reachable from it, push it onto a list. At the end, reverse the list.
Detecting cycles takes one extra piece of state: if the DFS ever meets an edge back to a node that is currently open, meaning you are still inside its call, that is a cycle.

Kahn's version is easier to reason about and gives you the cycle check for free. The DFS version is more compact if you already have a DFS in front of you and do not want the in-degree bookkeeping. Both of these algorithms run in
O(V + E)
time and
O(V)
space.

variants.code:
from collections import deque

def topological_sort_kahn(node_count, edges):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(node_count)]
    in_degree = [0] * node_count

    for before, after in edges:
        adj[before].append(after)
        in_degree[after] += 1          # one more thing blocking it

    ready = deque(v for v in range(node_count) if in_degree[v] == 0)

    order = []
    while ready:
        v = ready.popleft()
        order.append(v)
        for nxt in adj[v]:
            in_degree[nxt] -= 1
            if in_degree[nxt] == 0:
                ready.append(nxt)

    # Anything left un-emitted is stuck behind a cycle.
    return order if len(order) == node_count else None

content.text: Returning
null
rather than a partial order is intended behavior which signals that the graph contains a cycle.
Assuming the order is unique.
It usually is not, tests that compare against one specific expected order will fail on a perfectly correct implementation unless the problem pinned down a tie-break.
Skipping the count check.
Without it, a graph with a cycle returns a short list that looks like a valid order until something downstream breaks.
Forgetting isolated nodes.

A task with no dependencies in either direction has in-degree 0 and belongs in the output. If you seed the ready collection from the edge list rather than from every node, those nodes vanish silently.

questions.prompt: Kahn's algorithm emits 6 nodes on a graph with 8. What does that mean?

options.label: The remaining 2 are in or behind a cycle, so no valid order exists
The ready queue was drained too early
Two nodes had no outgoing edges

questions.prompt: What is a node's in-degree, in this context?

options.label: How many things must still be completed before it becomes available
How many tasks depend on it
Its position in the final order

questions.prompt: Your topological sort is correct but the grader rejects it. What is the most likely explanation?

options.label: Several valid orders exist and the grader wanted one particular tie-break
In-degrees were computed on the wrong nodes

questions.prompt: In the DFS version, why does reversing the finish order give a valid topological order?

options.label: A node cannot finish until everything downstream of it has finished, so reversing puts it before them
DFS visits nodes in order of in-degree
The finish order is already correct and reversing is a convention
